extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (especially those studying William James, Bergson, or theories of mind and metaphysics)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and formulating philosophical positions about mind, consciousness, and metaphysical unity vs. plurality, especially with respect to intellectualism and Bergson's alternatives. Focuses on logical consistency, explanatory power, and fidelity to lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candid acknowledgement of objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers should mention and confront the objections that have stopped others instead of ignoring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James criticizes monists who 'simply ignored' objections that had stopped him; Fechner is praised for candidness, while later writers like Royce are faulted for passing by objections in silence. The ideal is intellectual honesty: state known difficulties and respond rather than omit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with the experiential character of mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts that attribute experiential (mental) character to existence must reconcile that attribution with any claim of identity between higher and lower forms of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James points out the tension between saying 'mental existence is sentiri/experiri' and claiming the higher and lower are entitatively identical—if a mental fact is 'just pain' to some subject, a theory must explain how that same fact can simultaneously be the 'all' without changing its experiential character or else provide an alternative unifying mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a unifying agent or reject the naive 'as-appearing-so-it-is' thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: If one keeps the thesis that mental states are as they appear, one must admit a distinct agent of unification (an all-knower) to account for collective awareness; otherwise the thesis must be refuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James uses the 'joint-stock company all shareholders and no treasurer' metaphor: either posit an agent (analogous to a treasurer/director) who knows the parts together, or abandon the idea that appearance exhausts being. Discusses transcendental ego of apperception and its insufficiency if treated only as an all-witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asserting identity when forms of appearance differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim literal identity between the 'all' and its 'eaches' when the modes of appearance or experience they involve are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James: 'If their forms of appearance are so different, the all and the eaches cannot be identical.' The recommended move is to recognize distinct orders of witness (pluralism) or else provide a principled account of how differing appearances are nevertheless one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual coherence about points of view and aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory uses different 'points of view,' 'aspects,' 'quâ absolute' vs 'quâ relative,' or similar distinctions, it must coherently explain whether these denote different beings/orders of witnessing or are merely linguistic variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James argues that on idealistic principles such distinctions are tantamount to positing different beings; a coherent account must either accept plural witnesses or explain how such distinctions do not introduce ontological plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend claims of collective/distributive identity explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that a collective experience is identical with its constituent distributive experiences, a theory must provide logical grounds for that identity rather than treating the identity as obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James emphasizes that collective and distributive concepts are different; the burden is on the defender of identity (e.g., defenders of the Absolute) to show how the two concepts can be identical without contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory sufficiency over verbal placeholder concepts (avoid empty substantialism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid relying on traditional substantial terms (like 'soul') as mere stop-gaps; terms should carry genuine explanatory or pragmatic content rather than acting as placeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James contends that 'soul' often functions like other unrepresentable substances: 'without exception all so barren that to sincere inquirers they appear as little more than names masquerading.' If reintroducing such terms, show their pragmatic significance and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let conceptual definition trump sensible reality (criticize intellectualism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts and definitions are human-made extracts and should not be treated as superior or as the final determinants of what reality is; do not deny sensible properties merely because they don't follow from definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James traces intellectualism from Socrates/Plato: when definitions are privileged, one is tempted to deny change, connection, or properties not derivable from definitions (e.g., Hegelian moves). The correct method recognizes concepts as tools, not ultimate reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid categorial privation (denying properties because not in definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists should not use the absence of a property in a definition as a reason to assert its absence in the concrete object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: intellectualistic denials such as 'change is unreal' or the paraphrase 'a horseman can never go on foot.' James warns against 'unerbittlich consequent' logic that derives absurd denials from rigid definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for continuity/discontinuity across successive fields of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories must explain how successive fields of experience—each knowing the same matter in widening contexts—can have a common being or continuity rather than producing an unintelligible discontinuous universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James finds the regular succession of fields 'an unintelligible miracle' if they have no being in common; a satisfactory theory should show how continuity of being is maintained (or justify why not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance logical scruple with other kinds of rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: While logic has an 'imperishable use,' it should not be treated as the sole arbiter of what reality may be; one may need to give up or revise ordinary logic to account for lived reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James describes his personal move to 'give up the logic' influenced by Bergson: reality (where things happen) may be non-rational or supra-logical in the intellectualist sense. If proposing such a shift, provide an account and defend it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenological fidelity in accounts of time and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of time and motion should respect how time and change are felt (e.g., as discrete pulses or 'drops' of perception) rather than imposing an intellectualized, infinitely divisible continuum that produces paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Zeno's paradox and Bergson's critique, James argues that felt times 'come to us in drops' and that intellectual decomposition into infinitely divisible instants leads to antinomies; philosophical accounts should either show how such decomposition maps to experience or adopt a model aligned with phenomenology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value lucidity and expressive skill in philosophical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of expression and a style that follows the thought without obscuring it are important virtues in philosophical writing and aid persuasion and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James praises Bergson's 'lucidity' and 'phenomenal' expressive resources, noting that style can 'seduce' readers and make difficult ideas accessible. Philosophers should cultivate explanatory lucidity alongside rigorous argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concepts instrumentally, not reified as ultimate entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat abstract concepts as useful extracts ('flowers gathered') from the stream of experience, valuable for practical purposes but not to be reified as changeless essences of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James: concepts are 'moments dipped out from the stream of time' and 'have no value but these practical values.' Theorists should avoid treating conceptual schemes as exhaustive accounts of concrete reality.
